new_public_evidence.source: Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo Path Simulation, Operations Research 56(3), 2008
new_public_evidence.result: Under the paper's Lipschitz-payoff/Euler assumptions, multilevel coupling reduces O(epsilon)-accuracy cost from O(epsilon^-3) to O(epsilon^-2(log epsilon)^2).

new_public_evidence.source: Cerou & Guyader, Adaptive Multilevel Splitting for Rare Event Analysis, 2007
new_public_evidence.result: Adaptive splitting targets regimes where crude Monte Carlo is unreasonable for extremely small probabilities, automatically chooses levels, and in the one-dimensional analysis retains the asymptotic variance of fixed-level splitting with small additional cost.

new_public_evidence.source: Gozzo, Adaptive Multilevel Splitting: First Application to Rare-Event Derivative Pricing, arXiv:2510.23461v3
new_public_evidence.result: Version 3, revised 2026-01-08, reports up to 200-fold computational gains over standard Monte Carlo in tested rare digital-option settings while preserving unbiasedness; trajectory cloning uses adaptive score levels and fresh randomness after the branch point.

new_public_evidence.source: Cerou, Heas & Rousset, Adaptive Reduced Multilevel Splitting, 2023
new_public_evidence.result: Introduces adaptive rare-event splitting when the true score is expensive by using a surrogate score with certified error bounds and cost-aware critical levels. Numeric factor not imported from the retrieved abstract-level evidence.

derived_results.claim: For restartable stochastic evaluations of ultra-rare trajectory failures, adaptive multilevel splitting is a strong candidate alternative to independent brute-force episodes: concentrate computation on trajectories making measurable progress toward the rare set, clone at adaptive crossing levels, resimulate suffixes with fresh randomness, and retain corrected splitting weights for an unbiased probability estimate. External evidence includes up to 200x gain in a recent finance stress domain, but no AI/system adaptation is tested here.

For average/continuous metrics with coupled evaluator fidelities, multilevel Monte Carlo provides a distinct mechanism from transfer learning: estimate a cheap level plus paired fine-minus-coarse corrections, keeping high-fidelity bias correction explicit. Giles' theorem gives a complexity-order improvement in its SDE scope. This candidate requires correction variance to decay under coupling and should not be applied blindly to discontinuous rare failures.

A useful synthesis is to route ultra-rare trajectory events toward splitting and smooth expectation metrics toward coupled multilevel corrections, rather than using one proxy/sampling method for both. Certified-surrogate splitting is a separate candidate when even the rare-event progress score is expensive.

negative_or_scope_evidence: The 200x AMS figure is contract/model specific and must not be generalized to AI evaluation without a matched local test.
AMS efficiency depends strongly on a useful reaction coordinate/score and valid branch/restart semantics; enrichment without the estimator weights is biased.
MLMC requires strong cross-fidelity coupling and shrinking correction variance; discontinuous rare-event indicators can violate the favorable regime.
AMS and MLMC gains come from different regimes and are not multiplicative.
No AGI capability claim follows from either sampling mechanism.
